The Older Perceptions of the ‘Ulama About the Younger Generation — Unless They Keep Up with the Times, They May Become Objects of Ridicule Themselves—and Turn the Din into an Object of Ridicule as Well!

Sometimes, one cannot help but be astonished by the perceptions and assessments of many ‘Ulama regarding the present generation, particularly Generation Z and Generation Alpha. Their statements and perspectives make it quite evident how far behind many of them are in keeping pace with contemporary society and its realities.

It seems that they are still accustomed to judging the younger generation through the lens of the experiences, thought patterns, and realities of previous generations. Yet, unless they recognize the profound changes that have taken place over time in social thinking, the pursuit of knowledge, access to information, and the broader intellectual environment, they will not only struggle to understand the younger generation but will also find it increasingly difficult to establish meaningful communication with them.

We are now living in an age of information revolution and artificial intelligence. Today, even an eight- or ten-year-old child can use AI to find answers to various academic questions, learn new things about life and the world, and expand the boundaries of their knowledge.

My own eight-year-old son also uses AI to understand many aspects of his studies. In fact, some of the things he has learned from AI about the universe are entirely new even to me. In other words, technologies and sources of information that many of us are only beginning to explore have already become ordinary tools of learning for the younger generation.

Therefore, there is little room any longer for addressing the younger generation with the assumption that they are still ignorant, naïve, or easily influenced. The days when one could get away with presenting fabricated information, baseless claims, incoherent interpretations, or exaggerated statements before them are virtually over. On the contrary, those who continue to speak with such assumptions may themselves find themselves in embarrassing situations.

The reason is simple:

A single smartphone now opens up an enormous world of information before them. They can verify the truthfulness, logical consistency, and credibility of a statement within moments. Without even having to consult a teacher or an ‘Alim, they can learn about and explore many subjects that would have been almost unimaginable for people of our generation at their age.

There is one particularly important point that must be kept in mind:

Easy access to information does not necessarily translate into deep knowledge or wisdom. Differences in experience, judgement, and maturity may certainly exist between what the younger generation knows and what it is yet to fully comprehend. However, this is no justification for underestimating their intellectual curiosity, their willingness to ask questions, or their ability to verify information.

Rather, if we wish to engage meaningfully with them, we must also enrich our own knowledge and broaden our intellectual horizons in the light of contemporary realities. The assumption that someone is beyond questioning simply because of their age, institutional position, or religious identity is unlikely to find acceptance among this generation.

Therefore, responsibility, accuracy of information, and intellectual vigilance are more essential than ever when addressing the younger generation. This responsibility is even greater when speaking about matters of the Din.

The days when a statement could be established merely through emotional appeals, an air of authority, or religious credentials are gone. Every assertion must be supported by reliable information, coherent reasoning, and credible interpretation. One must also possess the intellectual honesty to acknowledge when one does not know something.

We must remember that serving the Din is not possible by belittling the younger generation, disregarding their right to ask questions, or presenting baseless statements. On the contrary, careless, irrational, and irresponsible remarks may turn the Din itself into a source of entertainment and ridicule in their eyes.

Times have changed, generations have changed, and the avenues through which information and knowledge are acquired have also changed. If the thinking of many among us remains trapped in the same old patterns, there is little wonder that we may become objects of ridicule in the eyes of the younger generation.

For the sake of preserving the dignity of the Din, cultivate the habit of knowing, understanding, and verifying before speaking.

**Do not turn the Din into an object of ridicule!**
